title: 5 Logical Fallacies to Spot in Arguments
summary: The creator explains five common logical fallacies—straw man, ad hominem, false dilemma, false cause, and hasty generalization—that make arguments sound convincing even when they do not make sense. The main lesson is to learn these fallacies so you can recognize flawed reasoning in everyday conversations.
key_points: Straw man: Taking someone's argument, changing it into something more extreme that they did not say, and arguing against that instead.
Ad hominem: Attacking the person making the argument rather than the argument itself.
False dilemma: Presenting a situation as if there are only two possible options when in reality there are more.
False cause: Assuming that because two things happened together or in sequence, one caused the other.
Hasty generalization: Taking a small or emotional piece of evidence and using it to support a much broader claim about an entire group.
content:
Logical fallacies are everywhere once you know what to look for #psychology #criticalthinking #logic #debate #biases

One of the best ways to become better at arguing with people is to understand logical fallacies, because once you know what they look like, you'll start to notice when an argument seems convincing, but it doesn't actually make sense. So here are five logical fallacies that you can spot in everyday conversation.

Firstly is a straw man. Now, a straw man is when someone takes your argument, changes it into something you didn't actually say, and then argues against that instead. For example, if you said, "I think we should reduce how much we're spending on social media advertising," and someone responds with, "So you think social media is completely useless?", that would be a straw man. You didn't say it was useless, but they've turned your argument into something more extreme because it's easier to disagree with. So when you hear someone responding to a version of your argument that you just don't recognize, that's a big clue.

Secondly is ad hominem, and that literally means to the person. So you'll see this when someone attacks the person making the argument rather than the argument itself. This could be something like, "You shouldn't listen to his opinion on climate change because he's not a scientist." Now, that might be relevant in some context, but it doesn't actually tell us whether or not his argument is correct. A more obvious example would be something like, "You're an idiot, so your argument is wrong." Being an idiot or being annoying, young, rich, poor, whatever, doesn't automatically make someone's argument false. So you must ask if someone is actually responding to the point, or if they're just trying to discredit the person making it.

Next, we have the false dilemma, and this is when someone presents a situation as if there's only two possible options, when in reality there are actually more. So for example, it could be something like, "Either you support this policy, or you don't care about the problem." Those aren't necessarily the only two options. You could think the problem is serious and also disagree with that particular policy. This one's especially common because it makes complicated issues seem really simple. So when you hear, "It's either this or that," in an argument, you must ask yourself if those are really the only two options.

This is probably the one I find most frustrating, and it's called false cause. It's assuming that because two things happened together, one of them caused the other. For example, "I started taking vitamin C and my cold went away, so vitamin C cured my cold." Maybe it did, but that doesn't necessarily follow from those things happening in that order; your cold might have just gone away naturally. This happens because our brains are really good at finding patterns and causes even when the evidence isn't enough to actually establish one. So if someone says X happened, then Y happened, so X caused Y, that's something to be suspicious of.

Finally, we have the hasty generalization, and this happens when someone takes a small piece of evidence and uses it to support a much broader claim than what the evidence actually shows. For example, "I had a terrible experience with one taxi driver, so all taxi drivers are terrible." You've taken one example and used it to draw a conclusion about an entire group. This is particularly easy to do when the example is emotional; one bad experience can feel more representative than it actually is.

The reason I think these are worth knowing isn't so that you can win every argument or start shouting "straw man" every 5 minutes; it's because they give you a really useful way of thinking about arguments. Start noticing why something sounds convincing, rather than just whether you agree with it. And honestly, once you learn these, you start spotting them everywhere.
